compounding_issues: No dependency manifest: bcrypt, PyJWT, celery, flask_limiter, and redis were added across sessions with no requirements.txt, so the final suite depends on undeclared external services.
Binary artifacts (__pycache__/*.pyc) committed in Session 1 and re-committed in every subsequent session — repo hygiene debt never cleaned even in the refactor session.
Dead code accrued and never removed: _legacy_format_date, _notify_admin stub, and fetch_task alias survived all 5 sessions including Session 4's refactor.

Session 2's owner_id signature change rippled through every model function and forced tests to be rewritten; the Session 4 refactor extracted SQL but left the email-notification trigger inline in the Flask route, keeping business logic coupled to the web layer.
add_task uses unguarded request.json['title'] (unhelpful KeyError/400) while every other route uses the silent get_json pattern — an inconsistency present from Session 1 that persisted to the end.
Session 5's Redis-backed flask_limiter had no storage fallback or test stub, so the added rate-limit tests fail without Redis and the story ends non-green (31/40).
key_decisions: Session 2 introduced an owner-scoped data model (owner_id column + idempotent ALTER TABLE migration) that established per-user data isolation as a core invariant every later session honored.
JWT + bcrypt auth behind a login_required decorator and g.current_user_id — the auth seam Session 5 later reused for per-user rate-limit keys.

Session 4's repository pattern (ABC BaseRepository + TaskRepository/UserRepository with injected get_db) removed ~113 lines from app.py and created the extension point (find_all_by_owner_paginated) that Session 5 built on.
Session 3 chose a real Celery async notification over the existing _notify_admin stub, using eager mode for testability.
Idempotent schema evolution (PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE guards) let feature sessions extend the schema without breaking existing data.
Session 5 added cursor-based pagination and flask_limiter rate limiting as the cross-cutting concerns, deliberately building on the repository layer.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily and structurally for the first four sessions: Session 1 established a clean scaffold with 12 passing tests, Session 2 added a coherent auth layer with per-user isolation and doubled test coverage to 24 green, Session 3 integrated Celery notifications cleanly (29/29), and Session 4 was a genuinely good refactor that reduced app.py by ~113 lines, introduced a repository layer, and held the suite green (29/29) with no regression. The arc broke at Session 5: pagination and rate limiting were added with 11 new tests, but the Redis-backed limiter had no test seam, so the story ended at 31/40 passing — the only non-green state in the sequence. Overall the architecture became cleaner and more layered over time; only the final cross-cutting session overreached by coupling the suite to an unstubbed external service.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent canonical arc (greenfield → feature → integration → refactor → cross-cutting) with steady architectural improvement through Session 4, marred only by Session 5 ending non-green because the Redis-backed rate limiter was added without a testability seam.
